question: The EU’s recycling industry has reported a sharp increase in the number of fires in collection vehicles and sites. Incidents caused by the improper disposal of lithium-ion batteries are reported on a daily basis in several Member States. As a result, insurers are backing out or significantly raising premiums or deductibles.

Critical waste management infrastructure is thus coming under increasing pressure, including as a result of these improper disposal practices and the strong demand for battery-powered disposable products, such as single-use e-cigarettes, lacking a functional take-back system.

At the same time, cheap imports from non-EU countries (some of which are primary goods but declared as ‘recycled’ products, others are recycled products manufactured under lower environmental standards) crowd out European suppliers and jeopardise investment in modern recycling. 1.

In the context of the Batteries Regulation, the Waste Framework Directive or a future circular economy act, what short-term initiatives – such as an EU-wide battery deposit scheme, a fire damage fund financed by manufacturers, or even a ban on single-use ecigarettes as already implemented in Belgium – is the Commission examining in order to prevent battery fires?

How does the Commission intend to put an end to distortions of competition caused by the declaration of primary products as recycled goods or by the import of goods recycled in non-EU countries without equivalent environmental or evidential standards, for example by means of strict evidentiary obligations, market surveillance, or trade or customs instruments?

What measures – including in relation to insurability, temporary support and investment in fire protection – is the Commission considering putting in place to stabilise recycling capacities and enhance the enforcement of the EU’s legislation on waste?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.12.2025) The Batteries Regulation1 addresses the entire life cycle of all batteries placed on the Union market including requirements to fully address the end-of-life stage.

To this end, the Regulation mandates high collection rates for portable and light means of transport batteries2, which, due to the separate collection and proper treatment, will result in a reduction of fire risks. The Regulation will increase the mandatory removability of batteries from appliances by February 20273, which will also reduce fire risks due to batteries left in appliances.

In line with Article 63 of the Regulation, the Commission will assess the feasibility and potential benefits of establishing deposit return systems for batteries by the end of 2027. The Commission will provide a report to the European Parliament and the Council and consider appropriate measures.
Furthermore, the Regulation4 applies to newly manufactured batteries but also to second-life batteries, except where explicitly stated otherwise in the Regulation itself.

In line with Article 8 of the Regulation, the Commission is currently working on developing the methodology for calculation and verification of recycled content of certain metals in batteries, including specific rules for third-party verification by notified bodies.

With regard to measures to insurability and support in fire protection, the Commission considers that national initiatives such as financial contribution for fire prevention measures in waste management facilities could be pursued at the operator or Member State level.
The organisation of logistics at local or operator level such as improved sorting infrastructure could provide the proportionate response to prevent fires due to batteries.
1 Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 July 2023 concerning

batteries and waste batteries, amending Directive 2008/98/EC and Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and repealing Directive 2006/66/EC, OJ L 191, 28.7.2023, p. 1–117. 2 Articles 59 and 60 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542. 3 Article 11. 4 in accordance with the Union framework on product regulation.
